From: Tom Reynolds <tom@correlate.ai>

Date: Wed, 21 Apr 2027 15:05:00 -0700
Subject: Dedicated sizing: first-pass telemetry and burst question

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for the intro — excited to evaluate Redwood Dedicated for our inference tier. I attached a recent telemetry dump from last week (minute-level aggregates) and a short note on our production behavior. High level:

- Baseline QPS: ~120 RPS sustained during business hours (PST).
- Night baseline: ~8–12 RPS.
- Daily scheduled batch jobs (03:30 UTC) cause periodic spikes lasting 8–12 minutes.
- Unpredictable bursts: roughly 2–3 times/week, we see sudden surges to ~1.6k RPS for 30–90s.

Model mix: mostly GPT-family open model variants (13B-ish) with a smaller 7B fallback for cheap inference. Typical prompt length ~120 tokens, average generated response ~340 tokens. We stream responses to clients.

Questions for you: what level of detail do you need on burst shape vs. aggregate QPS to recommend an autoscaling/burst policy and GPU mix? Also: is session stickiness required for KV cache benefits?

Appreciate any template you can send to structure the telemetry.

Cheers,
Tom
[Attachment: correlate_telemetry_snapshot_20270421.csv (CSV, 86 KB)]

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Dedicated sizing: first-pass telemetry and burst question

Hi Tom — thanks for the snapshot and the context, this is super helpful.

Quick answers up front:
- We prefer a short per-minute or per-5-minute histogram of requests (not just averages) to understand burst shape — percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99) and burst duration distribution are the most actionable.
- Session stickiness helps with KV cache hit rate and can materially reduce token cost for long-lived sessions; it is not strictly required but we recommend it when reuse > ~20% between client messages.

I attached a small CSV template (burst-profile-template.csv) — please fill the per-minute columns for a representative 7-day window if possible. The fields we use in sizing: timestamp, requests, avg_prompt_tokens, avg_response_tokens, model_tag, success_rate, latency_p50/p95/p99.

Couple of clarifying questions so we size GPUs and autoscale behavior:
1) For the unpredictable 1.6k RPS surges, are those single large jobs fan-out across many users or a few very high-throughput API keys?
2) What percent of overall traffic is request/response pairs that require streaming (i.e., token-by-token) vs. server-side batch generation where you accept higher latency?
3) Any constraints on acceptable P99 latency during bursts (e.g., must stay <500ms) or a cost-first leaky-bucket acceptable policy?

CC'ing Dev for implementation details and Ben for pricing/Reserved capacity planning.

If it's easier, we can hop on a 30-min call today — slot at 10:30am PT works for me.

Best,
Kimberly
Kimberly Park

Kimberly — thanks, attaching a 48-hour sample we've exported per your CSV header. Quick answers inline:

1) The 1.6k RPS surges are a mix: ~70% originate from automated client-side pipelines (many API keys simultaneously) and ~30% from a few high-volume enterprise partners.
2) 85% of requests are streaming-critical (clients expect partial tokens as they arrive); 15% are bulk batch jobs that can tolerate higher p99.
3) We don't have strict latency SLAs today — internal goal during bursts is p95 < 1s; p99 creeping up to 2.5s is currently tolerated but we'd like guidance on tradeoffs.

Notes: our average prompt/response distribution in the sample: prompt p50=110, p95=260; response p50=320, p95=620.

Attached: correlate_telemetry_snapshot_20270421.csv (48h sample) and a short README with column semantics. Let me know if the 7-day export will help; we can pull that but will take ~2 hours.

Thanks Tom — useful numbers. A few technical clarifications to help the sizing model and GPU mix recommendation:

- Model family & quantization: are you planning to run the 13B variant in FP16/AMP or an 8-bit quantized build in prod? We size differently if quantized kernels are required.
- KV cache reuse: can you estimate percent of requests that are from the same session within a 10-minute window? If >20–30% we will factor session-affinity into node pinning recommendations.
- Expected concurrency per connection: do clients open long-lived websockets or many short HTTP connections? Websockets raise concurrency per server but reduce repeated model load overhead.

From an ops perspective, with your burst shape (sub-minute spikes to 1.6k) we'll likely propose a hybrid: Dedicated reserved pool sized for the high-fidelity baseline + a configurable pre-warmed burst pool (GPU-accelerated) that can absorb the 30–90s surges with fast scale-up. We'll propose an autoscale policy that prefers routing to smaller quantized variants under heavy stress.

Ben — can you draft a preliminary reserved+burst pricing sketch once Tom confirms quantization preference?

-Dev
Dev Patel
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
